title: Janapada of Gandhāra
capsule: Gandhāra was one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas of Iron Age northwestern South Asia, with twin capitals at Takṣaśilā (Taxila) and Puṣkalāvatī (Charsadda), straddling the upper Kabul and Indus valleys in present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan. King Pukkusāti (c. 550 BCE) was its most prominent ruler, defeating Avanti's king Pradyota and maintaining diplomatic contact with Magadha's Bimbisāra; Nagnajit, an earlier king, appears in both Buddhist and Jain sources. The kingdom ended its independence around 518 BCE when Darius I of Persia incorporated the region as the satrapy of Gandāra, confirmed by its listing in the Behistun Inscription. Taxila subsequently flourished as a major center of learning under Achaemenid and later Macedonian, Mauryan, and Indo-Greek rule.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territory around Taxila and Charsadda is well-established archaeologically; broader political boundaries for the 600–500 BCE Janapada period rest largely on textual inference.
